## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

The *Uppādanirodhavāra* (Ya 6.2.3) is a section of the *Yamaka*, the sixth book of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. Within the structural architecture of the *Yamaka*, this text belongs to the process division (*pavattivāra*), which systematically investigates phenomena through three primary analytical lenses: origination (*uppādavāra*), cessation (*nirodhavāra*), and simultaneous origination and cessation (*uppādanirodhavāra*) [Anderson 1999; Gal 2003; Ronkin 2005]. In this section, paired catechisms analyze the arising and ceasing of doctrinal categories across time—evaluating conditions in the present, past, and future, particularly with respect to persons and planes of rebirth [Nyanatiloka 2007; Anderson 1999]. Modern scholars note that the *Yamaka*'s *pavattivāra* sections, including the *uppādanirodhavāra*, represent an early milestone in Buddhist process metaphysics and the development of the theory of momentariness, introducing the subdivision of a moment (*khaṇa*) into distinct moments of origination and destruction (*uppādakkhaṇa*, *bhaṅgakkhaṇa*) [Gal 2003; Ronkin 2005].

According to DharmaNexus, the text shares extensive formulaic material internally with other Abhidhamma treatises, totaling 6,497 text matches across 34 Pali works [DharmaNexus]. Its closest textual parallels are the adjacent chapters within the same cycle, namely *Nirodhavāra* (Ya 6.2.2) and *Uppādavāra* (Ya 6.2.1), as well as corresponding *uppāda-*, *nirodha-*, and *uppādanirodha-vāra* sections in other chapters of the *Yamaka* (such as Ya 2, Ya 3, Ya 5, Ya 9, and Ya 10) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments automatically with several non-Pali Buddhist philosophical treatises, including the Tibetan translation of the *Arthaviniścayaṭīkā* (D4365) and Śāntideva's Sanskrit *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, though these represent machine text-reuse affinities rather than direct historical parallels [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records one modern translation of the text [SuttaCentral].
